title.value: Naulei on calling a tide twice that he had seen once

description.value: Interview with a tide crier of the weir order on the grammar of the flat call and the working of walls. Naulei describes asserting a tide as fact at a length holder's request.

content.value:
Q. If the tide were to come early, what would you call?

A. [calls] There. You have made me say it. I have now called an early water once, which is a proposal, and four people down the wall have stopped what they were doing. Do not do that again.

Q. We are sorry. There is no way to ask it?

A. Not in the call. Put your hand out like this and turn it and I will understand you and your recorder will get nothing, which is the arrangement.

Q. What is the difference between one call and two?

A. One is a proposal, two is a fact, three is a wall worked now, tools down, everybody. Three is not louder. Three is just three.

Q. Have you ever called two when you had one?

A. Once, in the season the forty-first length was slipping. The holder wanted the wall worked and would not have got it on a proposal.

Q. And the tide?

A. Came four days later than I said it. The wall got worked, which was the point, and the joint at forty-one to forty-two got closed in a hurry by people who were angry, and it has been the worst joint on the outer wall ever since. I have walked it every year and said nothing.

Q. Would you call it again?

A. I would call it three times and take what came, and that is a different answer from the one you asked for.

consentNote.value: Naulei gave named consent as the holder of the call, for the material on the grammar and for the account of the forty-first length, and asked that the survey never again put a conditional to a crier on a working wall. The point was taken.
